strengths: The paper addresses an important question: what latent structure multimodal contrastive learning can recover. Distinct, statistically coupled latent variables provide a useful modeling abstraction.
Synthetic experiments cover several distributional assumptions and violations, report high recovery metrics, and include three repetitions.
The proposed CLIP postprocessing is simple and shows promising practical gains across multiple backbones, ImageNet distribution shifts, and 11 few-shot datasets.
weaknesses: The central identifiability proofs rely on an incorrect optimization argument. Appendix D.1, Lemma 5.1 claims that the normalized contrastive objective has global minimum zero. However, collapsed embeddings already give zero, while a realizable density-ratio critic gives −2I(x;t), which is negative for dependent modalities. Moreover, its condition that positive-pair representations agree almost surely forces constant representations under the full-support vMF model, contradicting the claimed uniform representations. This invalidates the bridge used to establish Theorems 4.1 and 4.3.

The convex-body proof contains another substantive error. Under Eq. (7), a uniform p(zx) generally produces a nonuniform p(zt) because the truncated kernel's normalization depends on position. Appendix E.1 establishes only a limiting claim as λ approaches zero, then uses exact uniformity at finite λ in Eq. (43). Theorem 4.3 therefore does not follow. Corollary 4.4 also omits the non-Euclidean metric restriction introduced in Appendix E.2; Euclidean distances permit rotations beyond scaled permutations.

The theoretical justification for FastICA is incompatible with the hypersphere assumptions. A uniform hyperspherical distribution has dependent coordinates and is rotationally invariant, so ICA cannot resolve its arbitrary orthogonal mixing through coordinate independence. Section 5's local-isometry argument for transferring the convex-body result to normalized CLIP features is also heuristic and supplies no recovery guarantee.

The downstream experiments do not isolate the contribution of disentanglement. Appendix K changes representation dimensionality to 300 components for ICA and 160/200 for PCA plus ICA, without matched-dimensional PCA or whitening controls. At fixed whitened dimension, an orthogonal ICA rotation preserves cosine similarities and an L2-regularized linear probe's objective. Consequently, the reported improvements could arise from dimensionality reduction and whitening rather than independent-component recovery.

The real-data evidence does not establish identifiability. Selected CelebA traversals and improved classification accuracy cannot demonstrate recovery of unknown generative factors. Quantitative disentanglement measurements, attribute-leakage assessments, and comparable raw-CLIP/PCA traversal controls are missing. Counting visually identified attributes against FactorVAE and β-TCVAE does not provide a controlled comparison.

The causal contribution is insufficiently defined. An undirected statistical dependency does not itself specify intervention semantics or identify causal relationships. The analysis concerns statistical representation recovery, with the subsequent isometry arguments substantially inherited from Zimmermann et al. [67]. The claimed advance beyond DAG-based causal modeling is therefore not established.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete. Appendix K omits important synthetic-training details, including sample counts and optimization settings, and does not clearly specify which samples fit PCA/FastICA. Real-data results lack repeated-run uncertainty. These omissions limit confidence in the practical findings, which cannot compensate for the fundamental errors in the central theoretical claims.
